title: Sublimis Deus (1537)
hook: Pope Paul III declares Indigenous peoples free and rational, often ignored by colonists

segments.voice: Yesterday, Las Casas, the priest who read a line about the bread of the needy and gave up his laborers. Your line was he changed. Did you say out loud where you'd been wrong? Day eight hundred thirty-nine.

Some questions should never need asking. On the island of Hispaniola, a Dominican friar named Antonio de Montesinos climbed into the pulpit on a Sunday in Advent and put one to the Spanish settlers in front of him. Are these not men? Do they not have rational souls? Las Casas later wrote down the sermon and how angry the congregation was. Years afterward, the question reached Rome, and a pope answered it in writing. Today's word is the first two words of his answer: Sublimis Deus.
screen: `A FRIAR IN THE PULPIT.` → `ARE THESE NOT MEN?` → `ROME ANSWERS IN WRITING.`

segments.voice: Begin with the title. The letter is named by its first words, and they mean the sublime God, the God on high. The letter opens not with the Americas but with God, who made people able to know him. Next, the lie it names. Paul III writes that some, moved by the enemy of the human race, have claimed that the peoples of the West and South should be treated like dumb animals, as if unable to receive the faith, and used that claim to put them to work. The letter calls this out for what it is. Then, the answer itself. The pope declares that these peoples are truly human, able to understand and receive the faith, and that they may not be deprived of their liberty or of their property, even if they are outside the faith. And the faith is to be offered to them by preaching and by the example of a good life, not by force. Underneath it is a line the letter itself leans on: Jesus sending out his apostles. In the Douay-Rheims: "Going therefore, teach ye all nations." All, the pope writes, without exception, because all are able to receive the faith. Last, the gap. A letter from Rome is ink. In the colonies, men with land and gold had every reason to look away, and the bull's promises were resisted and, on the ground, often not kept. Las Casas and others kept pressing its point before royal councils. So Sublimis Deus is two things at once: a clear statement of what the Church said about human dignity, and a reminder that saying it is never the end of the work.
screen: `THE GOD ON HIGH.` · `A LIE CALLED BY ITS NAME.` · `FREE, AND OWNERS OF WHAT THEY HAVE.` · `INK, AND THE GAP AFTER IT.` · then, large: `TEACH YE ALL NATIONS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold Indigenous peoples in mind. Sit comfortably and breathe. Bring to mind the Indigenous peoples of the land where you are right now, by name if you know it, or simply as the people who were here first. Think of them now, not only long ago: families, languages, elders, children. If you pray, you can pray for them in your own words, or rest with the line the pope leaned on, all nations, without exception. If you don't, let them stay in your attention, as real and present as your own neighbors. The bell holds the time.
Sublimis Deus. The sublime God. A papal letter of Paul the Third declaring that the peoples of the Americas are truly human, free, and not to be enslaved. Today's word.
Your line: they are truly human. Today, catch one moment when someone is treated as a category, a crowd or a problem, and in your head give them back a face. Day eight hundred thirty-nine.

howItsDone: Catholics point to Sublimis Deus in Church teaching on human dignity; Indigenous Catholics and their bishops have cited it, alongside later papal apologies, when speaking about the history of the Americas.

fork.setup: you're Paul III. some claim the peoples of the Americas are like animals, unable to receive the faith, and so may be put to forced labor. what do you write?
options: that they are truly human, free, and owners of their property.
that the question should be left to the colonists.
that they may be enslaved until they are baptized.
fork.reveal: he declared them truly human and able to receive the faith, not to be deprived of liberty or property, and to be invited by preaching and good example.

original.note: Latin: the sublime God, the God on high; the letter's opening words.

trapdoor: what you thought: a Latin title for a Church document.
what it means: a pope's answer, years later, to the question Montesinos had asked: these peoples are truly human, free, and not to be enslaved.
what a scholar hears: the letter frames the denial of their humanity as the work of the enemy of the human race, and still its promises were often not kept.

sources.ref: Bartolomé de las Casas, History of the Indies, Book 3, chapter 4 (Montesinos's Advent sermon)

notes: Sublimis Deus paraphrased throughout (the enemy of the human race; 'dumb brutes'; truly men; liberty and property even outside the faith; preaching and good example). Confirm paraphrase against the Latin.
Montesinos's sermon (Hispaniola, Advent 1511) is known through Las Casas's History; 'Are these not men? Do they not have rational souls?' given as a paraphrase without quotation marks. Confirm.

The voice says the bull's promises were 'resisted and, on the ground, often not kept', following the index hook ('often ignored by colonists'). The related brief Pastorale officium was later annulled under pressure from Charles V; omitted. Confirm whether the Keeper wants it.
'Papal letters are named by their first words' (incipit): standard practice; confirm wording.
howItsDone: Indigenous Catholic use of Sublimis Deus; confirm or soften.

Editor (second pass): the general claim that papal letters are named by their first words is narrowed to this letter (voice and myth); the unsourced "into courtrooms ... for years" softened to "kept pressing its point before royal councils".

Auditor: Genesis 1:27 ('to his own image') was quoted three days earlier on day 836; replaced with Matthew 28:19, which Sublimis Deus itself cites ('Go ye and teach all nations ... all, without exception'), so the verse now comes from the letter. Large screen and practice follow. Trapdoor no longer says the bull answered Montesinos directly (the question reached Rome through others, e.g. Minaya and Garcés). Confirm Douay-Rheims wording of Matthew 28:19 and the paraphrase of the bull.
